# Cassava and its detoxification (`cassava_detoxification`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/agriculture.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Agriculture & food (`agriculture`)
- Core idea: Cassava (manioc) is a tropical shrub grown from stem cuttings whose starchy roots yield heavily on poor soil, survive drought and keep in the ground for a year or two until needed. All varieties contain varying amounts of compounds that release prussic acid (cyanide). Traditional processing of high-cyanide roots combines several stages such as peeling, grating, fermenting, pressing and roasting. Breaking up the tissue allows the compounds to break down; liquid removal and heating help carry the cyanide away. The variety and the full process matter. Neither taste nor a fixed soaking time establishes safety.
- Pitfalls:
  - Eating bitter cassava merely boiled, or shortening the processing in a famine: acute cyanide poisoning or lasting paralysis of the legs (konzo)
  - Assuming bitter and sweet kinds can be told apart by looking
  - Drinking the press liquid or reusing soaking water; both may contain cyanide
  - Living on cassava alone; it is almost pure starch with very little protein
- History: americas: c. 8000–6000 BC – domesticated on the south-western rim of Amazonia; staple of the Taíno, who gave Columbus cassava bread in 1492; africa: c. 1558 – introduced to Kongo by the Portuguese; spreads inland with the processing methods in the 17th–19th c.; india: 17th–19th c. – introduced to south India and Southeast Asia
- Read:
  - William O. Jones, Manioc in Africa (1959)
  - Charles C. Mann, 1493: Uncovering the New World Columbus Created (2011)
